title: Local AI vs Cloud AI
description: Trade-offs, privacy implications, hardware requirements, and when to run models locally vs via API.

data.text: The choice between running AI models locally on your hardware versus calling cloud APIs has shifted dramatically in recent years. Improved open-source models (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen), better quantization techniques, and more powerful consumer GPUs have made local AI a practical option for many use cases. But the right choice depends on your priorities: privacy, cost, latency, capability, or convenience.

Cloud APIs offer the strongest models, zero hardware investment, and instant scaling. Services like OpenAI's API, Anthropic's Claude, and Google's Vertex AI host models with hundreds of billions of parameters that would be impossible to run locally. You pay per token, get 99.9% uptime, and benefit from the provider's ongoing security and compliance certifications.

data.title: Cloud AI strengths:
items: Access to state-of-the-art models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini Pro)
No hardware required — works on any device with internet
Automatic scaling — handles traffic spikes without provisioning
Fast iteration — swap models with a config change

data.text: Local AI keeps your data on your machine, eliminates per-token costs, and works without an internet connection. Modern quantization techniques (GGUF, GPTQ, AWQ) can shrink large models to run on consumer GPUs or even CPUs with acceptable quality. For developers, researchers, and privacy-sensitive organizations, local AI removes the dependency on external providers entirely.

data.text: Local AI performance depends heavily on GPU VRAM. A 7B parameter model quantized to 4-bit requires about 5 GB of VRAM; a 70B model at 4-bit requires about 40 GB. Apple Silicon with Unified Memory is surprisingly capable — an M2 Max with 32 GB can run 7B models smoothly and 13B models acceptably.

Quantization reduces model precision from 16-bit floats to 4-bit or 8-bit integers. This shrinks model size by 2-4x and speeds up inference, but some information is lost. The question is how much quality degrades. For most practical tasks, 4-bit quantization of LLaMA-3-8B or Mistral-7B produces outputs nearly indistinguishable from full precision.

cards.title: FP16 (Full Precision)
cards.description: Original model weights with no quantization. Largest file size, slowest inference.

cards.title: 8-bit Quantization
cards.description: Half the precision. Good balance of quality and efficiency for most uses.

cards.title: 4-bit Quantization (GPTQ/AWQ)
cards.description: Aggressive compression using optimized quantization. Popular for consumer hardware.
cons: Minor quality loss on hard tasks

data.text: For low-volume use (under 100K tokens/month), cloud APIs are often cheaper than owning hardware. But for high-volume applications, local AI eliminates per-token costs entirely. A one-time GPU investment of $1,500-$3,000 pays for itself in months if you process millions of tokens.

data.title: Monthly cost comparison at different volumes
data.content:
Assumptions: GPT-4o-mini at $0.15/1M input + $0.60/1M output

| Monthly Tokens | Cloud Cost | Local (amortized) |
|----------------|------------|-------------------|
| 10M tokens | $1.50 | $125 (hardware amortized) |
| 100M tokens | $15.00 | $125 |
| 1B tokens | $150.00 | $125 |
| 10B tokens | $1,500.00 | $125 |

Local becomes significantly cheaper above ~100M tokens/month. Below that, the convenience of cloud APIs usually wins.

data.text: For regulated industries (healthcare, legal, finance), sending sensitive data to cloud APIs may violate compliance requirements. HIPAA, GDPR, and industry-specific regulations often require data to remain on-premises. Local AI eliminates this concern entirely — no data ever leaves your machine. Many cloud providers offer 'private' or 'enterprise' deployments, but these are significantly more expensive.

data.title: Even 'private' cloud deployments have risks
data.text: Some cloud providers offer data processing agreements and private VPCs, but you're still trusting their security practices. Local AI removes this trust requirement entirely. For organizations handling PII, PHI, or financial data, local AI is often the only compliant option.

data.title: Decision guide:
items: Choose cloud AI when you need the strongest models, don't have powerful hardware, or process sensitive data with trusted providers
Choose local AI when privacy is paramount, you process high volumes, need offline capability, or want full control
Use hybrid: run sensitive tasks locally and send non-sensitive tasks to cloud APIs
Consider team expertise: local AI requires GPU management, model updates, and infrastructure maintenance

terms.definition: Reducing model precision from 16-bit floats to 4-bit or 8-bit integers to shrink file size and speed up inference.
A popular quantization format for running LLMs locally, supported by llama.cpp and many inference engines.
Software that runs a model locally, optimizing for specific hardware (e.g., llama.cpp, Ollama, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM).

data.title: Summary
points: Cloud AI offers the strongest models and zero infrastructure cost
Local AI provides privacy, no per-token costs, and offline capability
Hardware requirements scale with model size: ~5GB VRAM per 7B model at 4-bit
Quantization trades small quality loss for large efficiency gains
Local AI becomes cheaper than cloud APIs at high volumes (100M+ tokens/month)
Hybrid architectures let you run sensitive tasks locally and non-sensitive ones in the cloud
data.takeaway: The local vs cloud decision isn't about which is 'better' — it's about which fits your constraints around privacy, cost, latency, and infrastructure expertise.
